stories.headline: Relative obscurity to pick 1 buzz: WA's Heath Mellody is the ultimate bolter
stories.summary: Heath Mellody was a relatively unknown prospect earlier in the year. But then the National Championships came around, and the Larke Medallist suddenly has open pool pick 1 buzz, writes Jasper Chellappah.
stories.body:
Heath Mellody was sporting a new look at the AFL Draft combine. Usually standing out with the long, curly locks flying through the midfield, the Hale School graduate was hard to recognise with a buzzed dome.

He and schoolmates in Perth shaved their hair in the name of brain cancer research to venerate a Hale student.

Ryan Murphy passed away in early 2023 from glioblastoma, an incurable brain tumour. Mellody and his friends have been paying tribute ever since, with all proceeds being donated to the Harry Perkins Institute of Medical Research.

It's become a tradition at a school that has meant so much to Mellody. He opted to play his state-based footy with Hale in the PSA over the Claremont Colts.

From representing Western Australia at the national championships to running out on Optus Stadium for the WAFL Grand Final, his stocks have just kept on rising.

"School, academy, state and WAFL, it's just been so good," Mellody told ESPN.

"I love playing PSA footy with all my schoolmates. I sort of realised it'd probably be my last time playing with them.

"I didn't want to take it for granted, just tried playing like I usually would, preparing the same for any game. I loved every game and just had so much fun playing with my mates."

With no vision of the competition and no data being captured by Champion Data it kept Mellody hidden through the first portion of the season. That all changed at the National Champs.

"I was playing predominantly halfback and in the trial games I was having more of a split, and I was always playing a bit better in the midfield.

"I was always planning on playing midfield for parts of the first two games but that just didn't eventuate. But just before halftime of the Marvel game (against Vic Country) I got moved into the middle.

"I definitely prefer playing inside and it was just super fun going in there. We sort of mixed it up a bit in there and it gave us a bit more intent, bit more run and carry which in the end really helped.

WA was trailing Vic Country 38-10 before his move on-ball. They then piled on nine goals to three in the second half to storm over the top in front of every recruiter in the country.

Mellody was the firestarter. He won hard balls through the middle and used his trademark dash to put speed on the ball in transition. His hands were lightning under pressure and he had some special moments forward of centre that will be ingrained in those recruiters' minds.

The then-17-year-old finished with 33 disposals in the biggest 'pick me' game of the year.

He ended his epic champs with the Larke Medal around his neck as the best performed player at the carnival, joining the likes of Will Ashcroft, Sam Walsh and Christian Petracca by winning the award.

In truth, Mellody has been a prospect in demand since blitzing the colts grand final last season as a bottom-ager when he collected 25 touches and kicked a beautiful goal breaking the paint of 50 in a Claremont triumph.

"I loved playing Claremont colts last year. Getting connection with Charlie Banfield and Cody Curtin, playing AFL now, and going up against Toby Whan and Fred Rodriguez on Optus.

"That was so much fun and playing well in that finals series gave me a lot of confidence to go out and perform well this year."

That ended up being his final game of colts footy for Claremont because he was immediately called up to the senior team for a finals run this year. The Tigers surged from the middle of the ladder to make an unlikely grand final against a Peel side loaded with Fremantle talent.

Their best player in that grand final run was a teenager that missed his debut phone call because he was in second period at school.

"Ash [Prescott], the coach, gave me a ring while I was at school so I didn't actually pick it up. He called during the first couple periods... The head of sport at Hale told me to go get my phone and give him a call back!

"I went and did that and he was like 'Yeah, you're playing this week'."

Mellody's run at league level included a best on ground performance against a West Coast reserves midfield boasting the likes of Elijah Hewett, Fin Macrae and Harry Schoenberg. He took them to task with 34 disposals and a goal as Claremont rolled into finals.

"The biggest challenge was just working around the physicality of it. Obviously I'm a little bit smaller so it's going to be hard for me to body up so just working around that, getting off body, getting on the move a bit.

"The transition to the midfield made it a lot more comfortable for me at the level."

Mellody is now on the precipice of the top five, and has genuine pick 1 buzz. He's the most in-demand WA prospect since Luke Jackson, and West Coast is right in the mix at pick 3.

Mellody's beautiful kicking action and insatiable appetite to run and deliver is ideal for the modern game. He takes the ball from inside to out with leg drive that's reminiscent of Bailey Smith, though prides himself on his ball use going inside 50 and can pull off miraculous kicks when given space.

It may well be the Eagles who call Mellody's name, but the Bombers or Tigers will have first call on the unflappable teenager.

"I don't really have a preference to be honest. I'd just love to go anywhere, whether that be staying home or going interstate. I feel like it would be super cool and a great experience going anywhere... I've got a lot of support around Australia so I'll be able to manage if I were to move."

stories.headline: Panthers' Brad Marchand could be back in 6 weeks after knee injury
stories.summary: Brad Marchand said Thursday he's glad his knee injury wasn't more serious as he rehabs.
stories.body:
FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. -- The left knee injury Florida Panthers forward Brad Marchand suffered during a game in early October had him initially concerned that his season or even his career could be in jeopardy, he revealed on Thursday.

Those fears were quickly brought under control; the Panthers soon learned that Marchand would be able to begin on-ice rehab work within a few weeks, which was the case. Marchand said Thursday he hopes to return to game action within the next six weeks, possibly a bit less.

"I've never been so happy to be out for this amount of time," Marchand said. "The injury could have been so much worse. I've never hurt my knee before. I didn't really know what to think when I went down. I thought it really could have a career-ending type deal or a season-ending thing. When I found out it was going to be, whatever, a couple of months, I was pretty happy that that was the case. It's been getting better every day and getting stronger and we're working through it."

Marchand was hurt in early October in a game at Los Angeles, when he took a high stick late in the second period and wound up crashing into the goal post. His left knee bent at an awkward angle and he had to be helped off the ice by teammates, unable to put any weight on that leg.

That came on the heels of Florida captain Aleksander Barkov getting hurt in the Panthers' second game of the season -- after he missed all of last season with a knee injury. Barkov is also nearing a return and has been going through workouts with Marchand to get ready.

"Hopefully, soon, both of us will be back and it's been obviously great to share the experience with Marchy and just to see him on a daily basis, what he does, how he gets ready and just everything, like getting to know him a little more," Barkov said. "I didn't think I would ever say that before -- but it's been great. He's one of a kind."

Marchand, 38, is in his third season with the Panthers after playing his first 16 seasons with the Boston Bruins -- one of the team's top rivals. He was traded to Florida in March 2025 and helped the Panthers win their second straight Stanley Cup that season.

Marchand is under contract for four more seasons after this, so the Panthers clearly feel he has a ton of hockey left to play. He said he's hopeful he can dictate when his time is done -- and not have an injury make the decision. That's why he's embracing the rehab, doing all he can to get back into games before too much longer.

"When you win, that's what drives you. I want to win," Marchand said. "It's always been about that. ... The longer you play, you realize that you may think that you are going to have multiple opportunities throughout your career -- and I've been fortunate enough to have a few -- but you may never have another one. The older I get, I realize how little time I have left, and you want to make the most of it."

Marchand, Barkov and Panthers hockey operations president and general manager Bill Zito were among those appearing Thursday at the unveiling of a newly designed Airbus A320 plane painted to pay tribute to the two-time Stanley Cup-winning franchise.

The plane, named "Go Cats Go," is painted in the team's red, with a Panther painted near the JetBlue logo. The team's shield is on the tail, and red letters spell out "FLORIDA" against a white belly underneath the plane.

Marchand was among those who signed the aircraft -- which was taking its first flight Thursday to Boston, his former home.

"It makes you feel a lot of pride," Zito said.

stories.headline: Soccer's main characters: Man United, Como, PSG, Donnarumma
stories.summary: What are we watching this week? Man United are hoping for a rally, Como are magical to watch, PSG are the team to beat and we're worried about Gianluigi Donnarumma.
stories.body:
It's getting ridiculous in the best possible way. With each passing year, seemingly as teams realize that the extended Champions League league phase offers plenty of leeway if they lose a game or two, the guardrails slip a little bit more.

In 2024-25, teams averaged 1.63 goals per game in the league phase, a robust amount but not dramatically off of what we see in domestic leagues. In 2025-26, it was 1.69.

This year, through four matchdays, teams are averaging 2.02 goals per match. On Wednesday alone, six of nine matches saw at least five combined goals scored.

There were three 3-2 matches, including Fenerbahce's comeback win over Liverpool and lovely back-and-forth away wins for Manchester City (over RB Leipzig) and Real Madrid (over AEK Athens). And of course, there was Como's eye-popping 9-1 in over poor Lens; in their first Champions League campaign, the Italian side have scored 19 goals in their first four matches, winning three.

- UCL Talking Points: Are Como the real deal?

- Yamal makes more history for ruthless Barcelona

- Soccer's rich history of fan protests

The lack of consequence certainly has something to do with all this swashbuckling play, but maybe it's rubbed off on the rest of Europe? The season is still young, but scoring is up 7.8% in Ligue 1, 8.0% in the Bundesliga, 10.0% in LaLiga, and a whopping 20.1% in the Eredivisie and 23.9% in Serie A. Most of the increase has come from open-play, too -- it's not like teams are just earning a lot more penalties or something. (Meanwhile, Premier League scoring is actually down 2% so far this season. Fuddy duds.)

This is certainly a trend worth looking into, but for now I just want to say ... thank you. Goals are fun.

Let's once again look at five of soccer's main characters following another rousing Champions League matchday.

Main character No. 1: Manchester United's path forward

Ninety minutes is a long time. It's easy to forget that when you're an American fan accustomed to 3½-hour American football games, but on Tuesday at Old Trafford, 90 minutes was long enough for Manchester United to play maybe their most listless 45 minutes of the 2020s (a high bar to clear), watch their fans rain tennis balls onto the pitch in protest of administrative incompetence and a nine-match winless streak, grab a lifeline in the form of a penalty, miss said penalty, take advantage of a second chance via VAR, spend a good 20 minutes blowing a number of great chances to tie, and still have enough time left to tie, take the lead and hold on for what might (or might not) be a season-saving and trajectory-defining win.

Roma's two early goals made United look completely hapless, and when United fell behind 2-0, it almost looked as if Bruno Fernandes started trying to pick a fight and land a red card so he wouldn't have to watch the rest of the match. It even took Fernandes a second penalty attempt to get the home team on the board.

But from the moment his retake went into the net, Old Trafford seemed to flip into Fergie Time mode. Gone (for now) were the complaints and protests; back was the deep, guttural boom that stadium can generate when the home team scores a huge, late goal.

Roma have suffered some serious late-game issues in Champions League play, blowing a one-goal lead in a draw at Fenerbahce and now blowing a pair of two-goal leads in outright losses to United and Real Madrid. They've led in all four matches, but have just four points to show for it, and they certainly played a major role in their own demise Tuesday.

Still, something like this can definitely light a fire. Or at least, it had better.

While the entire Michael Carrick tenure looks a little different after Tuesday night's display, and the win kept their winless streak from reaching double digits, United's upcoming schedule is still pretty brutal: This Sunday, they host Aston Villa (who had a nice hot streak going before taking one on the chin against Barcelona on Tuesday), and when they return from the international break they visit Liverpool and Sporting CP, host Brentford and visit an equally desperate Newcastle. Without a major upgrade in form, the good feelings from this match won't last an incredibly long time.

During United's nine-match winless streak, the team suffered elements of poor fortune, scoring only six goals from shots worth 9.9 xG and allowing 18 from shots worth 16.6. But that isn't massive, and United had at least a slight negative xG differential in every game of this stretch. They were genuinely poor, and that obviously reflects on Carrick to some degree.

I actually liked the idea of making Carrick the full-time manager early on in his interim tenure last season, if only because he wasn't some overpaid Great Man type of manager -- the type that United typically try to hire -- and with Carrick in charge, the club might actually pursue a more sustainable roster-building strategy that isn't based entirely on the whims of said Great Man.

Carrick is simply a coach, and I thought that might work better. It certainly hasn't in 2026-27.

Still, it's not Carrick's fault that the club has spent so poorly in both the short and long term. It's not his fault that his left back options are either an injury-prone 31-year-old (Luke Shaw), a right back (Diogo Dalot) or a young center back (Ayden Heaven). It's not Carrick's fault that €75.9 million addition Carlos Baleba has managed only 397 minutes because of injuries (and just got hurt again), and it's not Carrick's fault that the club is, according to the estimates at FBref.com, paying Benjamin Sesko, Matthijs de Ligt, Harry Maguire, Mason Mount, Shaw, Noussair Mazraoui, Lisandro Martinez, Manuel Ugarte and Joshua Zirkzee nearly $100 million per year to not play close to the level required.

Carrick has gotten more out of players such as Bryan Mbeumo, Matheus Cunha, Kobbie Mainoo and even Fernandes than the last Great Man hire (Ruben Amorim) did. And while this is probably a lost season regardless -- United aren't winning the Champions League, and per the Opta projections they have only a 9.5% chance of finishing even in the Premier League top 7 -- it would benefit the club to not jump back into the Great Man waters just yet. But that will probably require Carrick generating quite a bit more magic in the coming weeks.

Main character No. 2: PSG and the biggest movers

Villarreal thumped Napoli and lost track meets against Borussia Dortmund and Liverpool to start Champions League play. They probably didn't expect to beat Paris Saint-Germain at home on Tuesday, but PSG were without star attackers Khvicha Kvaratshkelia and Ousmane Dembele, midfielder Marquinhos and also Nuno Mendes, maybe the best left back in the world.

Maybe they could keep things fun and competitive?

Nope. PSG led 4-0 after 17 minutes and rolled 6-0.

Even without that star power, they fielded a lineup loaded with Desire Doue, Maghnes Akliouche and Senny Mayulu up front, world-class midfielders Vitinha, Fabian Ruiz and Joao Neves and right back Achraf Hakimi, the best right back in the world. They brought World Cup-winning goal scorer Ferran Torres off the bench, and they got a goal from 17-year old fullback David Boly.

This is getting unfair. PSG at least made other teams think they had a chance the last couple of Champions League campaigns, easing into the league phase each year before shifting into gear when it counted. This time around, they've won their first four matches -- including matchups with Manchester City and Barcelona -- by a combined 20-5. Manager Luis Enrique is rotating as heavily as he ever has early in this season, both because of injury and because he wants to, and they've won 10 straight in all competitions by a combined 36-9. And the two-time defending Champions League winners' expected league phase point totals, per Opta's power ratings, have improved more than anyone else's in the competition.

Finally, those plucky Paris underdogs find some traction. Life's been so hard for them lately.

Three other teams have seen their expected point totals rise by at least 4.4 points: Real Madrid, who are also off to a perfect start -- albeit one full of late-game drama (and three one-goal wins) -- plus the ever-delightful Club Brugge and a Real Betis team that was off to a perfect start until Wednesday's 2-1 loss at Borussia Dortmund.

The biggest drops aren't quite as stark, primarily because they've all come from teams that weren't expected to do so hot anyway: Slavia Prague (down 4.2 points), Lille (3.9), AEK Athens (3.0) and Slovan Bratislava (2.6) have combined for one win and five points in 16 matches, though Slavia did frustrate Arsenal in a competitive 2-1 loss on Wednesday. It wouldn't be entirely surprising if one of these teams found their footing and made a run in the second half of league play, a la Bodo/Glimt last year.

OK, it would be a little surprising.

Others with higher expectations certainly haven't enjoyed the starts they were looking for: Porto (down 2.8) lost their first three before thumping Napoli on Wednesday, Roma (down 2.5) have suffered the aforementioned late-game collapses and have one win despite leading every match, and of course Manchester United (down 2.1) have had their well-publicized issues.

Main character No. 3: How the hell does a team score nine goals?

You can ask Manchester United: Como can play some pretty sexy ball sometimes. Even while balancing the rigors of domestic and continental play for the first time, they've lost just two of their first 14 matches in all competitions, and they've scored at least two goals 10 times and at least four goals four times. They've pummeled United and RB Leipzig and beaten Napoli away.

Cesc Fabregas seems to know what the heck he's doing as a manager, and his squad has enough fun attacking talent -- 22-year-old Nico Paz (six goals and eight assists in all competitions), 23-year-old Martin Baturina (five and two), veteran center forward Anastasios Douvikas (11 and one) -- that they've barely missed a more established player like Moise Kean, who's injured and has played only 158 minutes.

It's clear that this is a good team. But they scored nine goals Wednesday! On the road! Against a team from a Big Five league (albeit the fifth one)! How is that possible?

I guess the short answer is, "They couldn't miss." Como attempted 18 shots worth a massive 4.3 xG -- elite in its own right (and shameful on Lens' part) -- but overachieved that xG by 109%. Douvikas attempted three shots worth 1.7 xG and put all three in the net.

For the longer answer, however, I went to the film. They weren't just sending in lucky screamers from 30 meters - every shot they scored on was worth at least 0.12 xG, and all but one was from within 12 meters. This was a clinic in shotmaking, so I wanted to walk through each goal. You can follow along here:

- Goal No. 1, seventh minute: Douvikas from 3.0 meters (assist by Maximo Perrone). A short corner exchange sets up a cross to the far side, where Perrone heads it toward goal; he doesn't get much on it, but his shot becomes an assist for Douvikas, whom Lens tried to claim was offside.

- Goal No. 2, 32nd minute: Douvikas from 5.7 meters (assist by Alex Valle). On a quick transition, Paz gets the ball with space on the far right. He fires in a long and pretty off-target pass to Valle, but Valle saves it from going out of bounds and the flat-footed Lens defense doesn't notice Douvikas right in front of the goal for the tap-in.

- Goal No. 3, 40th minute: Paz from 10.0 meters (assist by Douvikas). A quick transition from Lucas da Cunha to Valle to Maxence Caqueret to Douvikas, and suddenly Paz has far too much space on the right. He fires into the top shelf, then pays tribute to fallen Spanish forward Jesus de Miguel.

- Goal No. 4, 47th minute: Lucas da Cunha from 12.1 meters (assist by Paz). After a good 30 seconds of possession, it's Paz to da Cunha to Yan Couto to da Cunha to Paz to a breaking da Cunha. Maybe the prettiest goal of the night, and Lens are officially broken.

- Goal No. 5, 53rd minute: Marc-Oliver Kempf from 8.1 meters (assist by Luis Milla). Caqueret quickly fizzes a ball to Luis Milla out on the left. He just as quickly fires a cross into the box, and Kempf heads it in.

- Goal No. 6, 57th minute: Douvikas from 15.6 meters (assist by Paz). After a series of horizontal passes near midfield, Como quickly go vertical and catch Lens flat-footed -- Perrone to Paz to Douvikas for an instant transition goal.

- Goal No. 7, 62nd minute: substitute Mattia Liberali from 10.8 meters (assist by Jacobo Ramon). More instant transition as Ramon simply frees Liberali on the right, and the 19-year-old races into the box and fires. Paz, Douvikas, Da Cunha and Milla have been subbed out, and Como continue to pour it on.

- Goal No. 8, 69th minute: substitute Martin Baturina from 11.9 meters (assist by Liberali). Shortly after Lens finally score, it's Baturina to Liberali, quickly back to a racing Baturina. Como played right through the middle on Lens, over and over.

- Goal No. 9, 90+1 minute: substitute Matteo Papaccioli from 11.7 meters (assist by Liberali). More fun interplay from the subs. After some quick passing, Liberali finds the 18-year-old Papaccioli in behind, and he converts. It's initially ruled offside, but it eventually counts.

My conclusion after all that is basically the same as how I started this section: Como play some sexy ball. Quick touches, lots of angles, lots of good chemistry. Lens had no idea where to look.

Watch this team whenever you can.

Main character No. 4: What's wrong with Donnarumma?

Gianluigi Donnarumma has been a celebrated shot-stopper since he forced his way into the AC Milan lineup 11 years ago at age 16. He hasn't ever been elite with his passing, but even possession-hungry clubs like PSG and Manchester City craved his services because of how well he keeps ball from going into net.

Over the past five seasons, he's been mostly excellent in this regard. Using Stats Perform's Goals Prevented measure -- which looks at the post-shot xG totals keepers face from shots on goal and compares that to the number of goals they allow -- he's been well on the positive range in all competitions.

See if you can spot a recent development.

Donnarumma's goals prevented, last 5 seasons

- 2021-22 (PSG): +5.0 (positive is good)

- 2022-23 (PSG): +7.8

- 2023-24 (PSG): +12.6

- 2024-25 (PSG): +2.0

- 2025-26 (Man City): +6.8

- 2026-27 (Man City): -1.2

He's had some stellar games this season: He had three big stops in a 1-0 win over Coventry City, for example (+1.8 goals prevented), plus three more in a 2-1 win over Bournemouth (+0.7) and six in a 3-0 win over Liverpool (+0.7). But he's in the middle of a pretty dire stretch: In his last six games in all competitions, starting with City's 4-2 loss to PSG, he's at minus-4.0 goals prevented. Simply breaking even might have turned losses to PSG and Aston Villa into draws, and he was relatively poor again on Wednesday against RB Leipzig, allowing two goals from shots on goal with a post-shot xG of 2.0.

City did hold on to beat RBL, but they've still lost three of their last seven matches in all competitions, and they've allowed 12 goals in those seven. I'm not going to pretend seven matches is a sign of his end as an elite goalkeeper, but it's been a costly stretch, and if not for City's offense, it would be even more costly.

Main character No. 5: The midway point best XI

Even if the league phase is entertaining but reasonably disposable content, I still enjoy taking a moment to celebrate awesome players from time to time, so since we're at the midway point of this phase, here's a quick Best XI for the competition to date.

Goalkeeper: David Raya, Arsenal. It's hard to evaluate Raya because he doesn't typically have much to do behind Arsenal's defense, but he's saved 10 of 14 shots on target for a solid +1.8 goals prevented, and he has decent involvement in the buildup game. He had to make four saves against a game Slavia squad on Wednesday, but did so. Backup: Yann Sommer, Club Brugge

Right back: Achraf Hakimi, PSG. I could tell you his stats -- one assist, 12 chances created, 57 line-breaking passes received (most of any defender) -- but "best right back in the world" should do. Backup: Givairo Read, Feyenoord

Center back: Mykola Matvilenko, Shakhtar Donetsk. He's completed 57 progressive carries (second among defenders) and 36 progressive passes (fifth), and he has 1,401 meters of carry distance (first). The 30-year-old is a stabilizing force and strong buildup guy for a team currently in position to advance. Backup: Pau Cubarsi, Barcelona

Center back: Dayot Upamecano, Bayern Munich. Upamecano's another hard-to-evaluate player because he's put on such islands in Bayern's high-line system that you can probably remember him in the middle of a lot of breakdowns. But he's in those awkward spots because he's such a trustworthy 1v1 defender, and he's a high-level passer too. Backup: Brandon Mechele, Club Brugge

Left back: David Raum, RB Leipzig. Among defenders, Raum is third in chances created (10), eighth in progressive passes (34), second in crosses (34) and second in tackle attempts (21). He's been busy for RBL's strained defense, but he's always a pretty important contributor in attack too. Backup: Joao Cancelo, Barcelona

Defensive midfield: Declan Rice, Arsenal. Most progressive carries of any midfielder (48), most progressive passes (63), most carry distance (1,487 meters), third-most line-breaking passes (54), even eighth-most ball recoveries (24). He's brilliant and indefatigable. Backup: Elliot Anderson, Manchester City

Central midfield: Fabian Ruiz, PSG. He has four goals (most of any midfielder), 14 shots (most), 283 passes received (most), 58 progressive passes (second-most) and 57 line-breaking passes (second-most). He seems to be getting better at 30. Backup: Vitinha, PSG

Attacking midfield: Nico Paz, Como. Maybe the player of the competition so far. He's scored three goals with five assists, he's received 60 line-breaking passes (only Lamine Yamal has more), and I mean, just watch him. He seems to make everyone around him more creative than they otherwise would be. (And he's only 22.) Backup: Jude Bellingham, Real Madrid

Right win: Lamine Yamal, Barcelona. Another no-brainer. He also has seven combined goals (three) and assists (four), and he's received the most line-breaking passes (73), attempted the most ground duels (70) and won the most 1v1s in the box (five). He's even made the most ball recoveries in the attacking third (nine), including an easy one for a goal on Tuesday.

He's the best winger in the world, and he's still just 19. Unfair. Backup: Bradley Barcola, Liverpool

Center forward: Harry Kane, Bayern Munich. I wanted to get a little creative and give this spot to someone other than the reigning Ballon d'Or winner, but Kane is tied for second in combined goals (four) and assists (three), he's attempted the most shots (20), and even with slightly below-standard finishing -- four goals from 4.1 xG -- he's just the most complete player up front right now. Backup: Tasos Douvikas, Como

Left wing: Desire Doue, PSG. He's seventh in the competition in combined goals (three) and assists (two), and he's only played 218 of 360 minutes. Explosive, creative, ridiculously confident and, yes, still only 21. Backup: Zlatko Tripic, Viking

stories.headline: São Paulo Grand Prix: 'Very grateful' Rafael Câmara thanks Haas for early home debut
stories.summary: Rafael Câmara thanked Haas for the show of trust in handing him an early Formula 1 debut at home in Brazil ahead of his full rookie season in 2027, but refused to be drawn on whether he will finish the season with the team.
stories.body:
Rafael Câmara thanked Haas for the show of trust in handing him an early Formula 1 debut at home in Brazil ahead of his full rookie season in 2027, but refused to be drawn on whether he will finish the season with the team.

The Formula 2 championship leader has been handed an earlier-than-expected start to his Formula 1 career.

The Brazilian was already due to replace Esteban Ocon in 2027, but his elevation to the team was accelerated after the Frenchman's sudden departure on the eve of the Mexico City Grand Prix last week.

The famous Interlagos circuit hosts this weekend's São Paulo Grand Prix, but it is uncharted territory for the Ferrari junior driver.

"It's the first time [driving there]," Câmara confirmed on Thursday ahead of his debut at the famous circuit.

"For now, it's been OK," he said about the pressure of driving at home. "I think it should be alright. Also, I think myself, I've always been, whatever people think about what's happening outside, it's never been a problem."

Japanese driver Ryo Hirakawa had replaced Ocon last weekend as the Japanese driver was at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriquez, while Câmara was back home.

Explaining the circumstances which led to his elevation, Câmara said: "I mean, I was very surprised. Definitely not a place where I would expect to do a debut in Formula 1. But just very happy for the opportunity, very grateful as well for the team to put their trust in me this week. So just trying to enjoy the home race and have some fun out there."

Hirakawa grabbed a shock point in Mexico last week to cap an impressive debut weekend.

The early elevation will put Câmara immediately alongside fellow Ferrari junior Oliver Bearman.

Their 2027 partnership has already been dubbed as an audition for a future Ferrari race seat.

When asked about that by ESPN in his own media session, Bearman said: "Of course, it's easy to make that kind of comparison.

"Honestly, I'm excited to have a teammate that's going to push me really hard and of course I've had that across the years.

- Kimi Antonelli to honour Ayrton Senna with special helmet at São Paulo GP

- 1980 F1 world champion Alan Jones dies aged 80

- Charles Leclerc to miss Brazilian Grand Prix media duty due to birth of baby

Esteban [Ocon] pushed me hard, but Rafa is also going to be a very strong competitor. For us as competitive people, as racing drivers, you want someone that pushes you to the next level.

"And that's the best way to get the most out of the team, for sure."

Bearman added: Of course I'll be trying to help him out as much as possible."

Câmara acknowledged that Bearman's benchmark will be the one he needs to follow as he gets up to speed with F1 this week.

"Ollie, in the past year, he's been always doing a good job," Câmara said of his teammate's benchmark. "So it would be someone that would be good to learn and to see what he's doing so I can also distract myself and try to put in place."

He added: "On my side, just really trying to learn as much as I can. There will be a lot of things going on, but I think on my side, really, I just try to see it as a positive note, just driving at home. It's something that I didn't do for a long time, so I'm just really trying to enjoy this weekend and just have some fun.

"Obviously it will be not easy, but yeah, I think just really what always helps for me is just really focus on my side, focus on my job, and make sure that every time you're learning and moving forward."

As it stands, Câmara is on the cusp of the Formula 2 championship, which concludes with rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi in conjunction with the planned end of the Formula 1 calendar.

However, with Haas now confirming Ocon will not return before the end of the season, Haas will need to decide between Hirakawa and Câmara to close out the year -- as per F1's rules, they've already hit the maximum of drivers they can race with, meaning there's no chance they can run reserve driver Jack Doohan.

Racing at the final two rounds -- which are still set to go ahead despite ongoing uncertainties over the Middle East -- would mean Câmara effectively sat out the chance to clinch the F2 title.

Asked if this was a possibility, Câmara said his only focus so far is on the Brazil weekend.

"I think there's something still to come, still in the future," he said. "So I think, like I said, there will be a lot of things going on this weekend. So at least we are trying to focus on the job on this weekend. These will be things that will speak to the future, we'll see what will happen."

stories.headline: Mikel Arteta: Viktor Gyökeres 'really needed' a good Arsenal performance
stories.summary: Mikel Arteta has admitted Arsenal forward Viktor Gyökeres "needed" a good performance after he starred in the 2-1 Champions League win at Slavia Prague.
stories.body:
Mikel Arteta has admitted Arsenal forward Viktor Gyökeres "needed" a good performance after he starred in the 2-1 Champions League win at Slavia Prague.

Sweden striker Gyökeres made one goal and scored the other in one of his best displays since joining Arsenal in July 2025.

The 28-year-old has played second fiddle to Kai Havertz this season and had scored only one goal before Wednesday night, in the Carabao Cup penalty shoot-out defeat at Fleetwood last month.

But against Slavia, Gyökeres laid on the opener for Noni Madueke before scoring a stylish second on a hugely encouraging evening in the Czech capital.

"I thought he was really good," Arteta told reporters. "It was a game we believed would be really good for him, for the demands the opponent puts in and the spaces he could use.

"He's done it really well, not just for the assist and the goal, but he was really connected to the team. It's really great news for him, because he really needed that performance.

"He did that really well, understood really well when to appear, when to threaten, because they leave people, they follow man-to-man in the midfield and leave spaces there.

"So when I said he was really connected to the team, that was another example. I thought he had a great performance alongside the goal and assist.

"I'd imagine every player wants to play every game, and Viktor is no different. The players need to impact the game like he has done when they get the opportunity, to show the level they can produce. It's really positive for the team."

- Arteta: 'A lot to learn' from Arsenal's 'sloppy' win over Slavia Prague

- Kuyt hails 'another miracle in Istanbul' after Fenerbahce beat former club Liverpool

- Haaland tells Man City to 'step up' after netting winner in Leipzig

Despite his lack of minutes on the pitch, Gyökeres has now contributed to five goals in his last five matches.

"I feel very good," he told Arsenal's website. "Obviously, I'm happy with the win and to contribute to the two goals."

Premier League leaders Arsenal are up to third in the Champions League table despite a wobble in the second half, when Wiktor Nowak's 90th-minute goal left them clinging on throughout stoppage time.

"A good feeling in the first half -- and then obviously in the second half, with how that went, maybe the feeling isn't as good. But overall, if you look at the first half, it's a good feeling," added Gyökeres.

"It's my job as a striker and of course I want to contribute every game when I'm on the pitch and want to be involved as much as I can in attacks.

"So far we've had a good run in the Champions League and in the league as well.

"At the stage we're in right now, we're in a good spot, but I think we're all clear on what we can improve and what we need to do to take the next step."

stories.headline: How the Atlanta Dream turned their franchise around in just five years
stories.summary: Five years ago, the Dream were the second-worst team in the WNBA -- making their Finals run all the more remarkable.
stories.body:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Just five years ago, the idea of the Atlanta Dream competing for the WNBA championship trophy would have seemed as unlikely as a rebound landing untouched next to Angel Reese.

So finishing within one victory of a title, as the Dream did in the WNBA Finals last week, says a lot about just how far the franchise has come since 2021. Even without the 2026 championship, what the Dream did in revitalizing their franchise is a story that shouldn't be lost in Golden State's celebration. Five years ago, the Dream were a mess. Now, they're contenders. That's something other WNBA franchises can look to.

"It's remarkable, really," Atlanta coach Karl Smesko said.

Consider how far the franchise was from this in 2021.

That was the year the Dream moved to Gateway Center Arena -- the smallest venue in the WNBA at 3,500 seats -- because too much of their longtime larger home (State Farm Arena, capacity 17,608) was vacant during games. The Dream had three different coaches that year, one resigning just before the season began to take a college job. Chennedy Carter, their lottery-pick selection from 2020, was suspended in July and never returned. They finished in second-to-last place in the WNBA at 8-24.

The team's most notable moment came not on court, but in a viral video of two Dream players throwing punches by a food truck outside an Atlanta nightclub.

Those were the low points. But behind the scenes, two big moves in 2021 helped spark a turnaround: an ownership change, led by real estate investor Larry Gottesdiener, and a new general manager, Dan Padover.

Reese was then a college sophomore with huge goals for her future. But it wasn't until this April that she knew those plans would intersect with the Dream.

"When I play with joy and I'm surrounded by people that just genuinely make me happy, I think I'm at my best," Reese said. "The organization has poured into me. To be in my third year [in the WNBA], this is obviously the best situation I've ever been in."

And even as Reese and teammates Jordin Canada and Allisha Gray sat somberly in the Dream's postgame news conference after Game 7, the joyful sounds of Ballhalla's celebration audible, they looked dissatisfied but not devastated.

"They changed my life," Reese said of the Atlanta players and staff. "And I'm just so grateful for them."

A 2008 EXPANSION TEAM, the Dream's first title hopes were led by another Angel -- 2009 No. 1 pick Angel McCoughtry. She led the Dream to the Finals in 2010, 2011 and 2013, but they were swept each time.

The Dream then missed the playoffs six of the next nine years. They won a then-franchise record 23 games in 2018, but lost McCoughtry to a knee injury Aug. 7 and lost 3-2 in the semifinals.

Without McCoughtry in 2019, the Dream averaged just 4,270 fans for home games, necessitating the move from State Farm Arena. That relocation was delayed a year because of the COVID-19 pandemic, when the 2020 season was in a "bubble" in Bradenton, Florida. By then, McCoughtry had left in free agency for Las Vegas.

The Dream's leadership became a focus for all WNBA players in the bubble when co-owner Kelly Loeffler sent a letter to commissioner Cathy Engelbert opposing the league's decision to display "Black Lives Matter" logos on the courts in Bradenton. Loeffler wrote "we need less -- not more -- politics in sports."

Loeffler was involved in a political race at the time, seeking to hold her U.S. Senate seat. The divide mushroomed into WNBA players campaigning for her opponent, Raphael Warnock.

"Being on the outside of the Dream looking in then, during that time everybody was rallying around them," said guard Jordin Canada, then with the Seattle Storm, of the bubble activism against Loeffler's continued ownership. "We wanted what was best for them and the W as a whole, and to see that transition into a more positive direction."

The situation was untenable, and the franchise was sold in February 2021 to Gottesdiener's group, which included former WNBA player Renee Montgomery.

"I believed the WNBA was an extraordinary opportunity, not just to grow the game of basketball," Gottesdiener said, "but to demonstrate what's possible when you invest in women."

Padover, who joined the Dream in October 2021, had worked for the Las Vegas Aces for three years, helping build the team that would become a three-time champion. He went from a franchise a step from the top to one with nowhere to go but up.

Padover started his WNBA career as a video coordinator with the New York Liberty in 2012, and he has credited former coach and GM Bill Laimbeer for helping him develop into a team executive. He cites this key from Laimbeer.

"If you can get your organization organized and you can take care of the players, you can start to establish yourself as a place that is respected," Padover said. "Under previous ownership, I think we were disorganized, and we didn't really have an identity.

"When I got here the goal was, 'Let's turn Atlanta back into a franchise that's respected throughout the WNBA community, one piece at a time, and that will allow us to be able to build something.' We started with things like player housing, staffing, and medical and player development."

THE OTHER PIECE was putting the right players and coaches in the building. Padover, who has been named the league's executive of the year three times, put his trade wizardry to use. He dealt the Nos. 3 and 14 picks in the 2022 draft and a 2023 pick swap to Washington for the No. 1 pick in 2022 to select Rhyne Howard.

"It was a huge boost of confidence," Howard said. "Obviously, when you get drafted, that means the team wants you. But to do it in the way that they did -- trading up to get me like that -- put no doubt in my mind that I was a piece that they were looking for to start this new journey, to start this new outcome that we're having."

The 6-foot-2 guard was Rookie of the Year and has since been a four-time All-Star. She averaged 17.7 points in the regular season this year and 16.3 in the playoffs. Howard won't recall Game 7 fondly -- she was limited to six points on 3-of-14 shooting -- but she took noticeable steps forward as a player in 2026, especially on defense.

Padover also got the steal of the second round in 2022 with forward Naz Hillmon, who became a full-time starter this season and has played more WNBA games than anyone from that draft class.

Subsequent huge deals came for guards Gray (2023) and Canada (2024).

"One of the things that I definitely took from Bill was not to be skittish to give up things in trades," Padover said. "If you're doing it to get a great player, it's always worth it, and don't be afraid to do that."

One of Padover's biggest moves in 2025 was bringing in Smesko, who had spent most of his career as a college coach, including 17 years at Florida Gulf Coast.

"Obviously, there was a changing landscape in college basketball, and I was at the point where a new challenge was needed," Smesko said of his decision to move to the WNBA. "It was Atlanta, and I love the city. And I thought there was the makings of a core that could compete for a championship."

Atlanta went 30-14 last season but lost in the first round of the playoffs. Padover used a trade to acquire the last key component. On April 6, the Dream obtained Reese from the Chicago Sky for future draft picks. Reese had become disillusioned with the Sky's direction and voiced her concerns near the end of the 2025 season. She believed in the Dream's vision, just as the players obtained before her did.

"I feel like the organization has gotten to a point where players want to come play for Atlanta," Gray said. "To be able to get Angel just speaks volumes of how the organization is run and how it really cares for players. The city of Atlanta is great. Great culture. The games just feel like one big family cookout, and everybody's welcome."

Reese proved to be the final and most essential ingredient. Other than a five-game skid June 24-July 4, the Dream -- who also added veteran DeWanna Bonner late in the season -- stayed consistent, finishing 30-14 again. Reese had the best offensive year of her career, averaging 16.4 points, plus 12.1 rebounds.

"She's made me look good all season long," Howard said. "And I'm sure she's going to continue to do that for the rest of her time here. Shoutout to her for coming in and being bought in. She's handled every challenge that we've thrown at her with grace."

This year's Finals games in Atlanta didn't come without hurdles -- facility conflicts with State Farm Arena meant one Finals game had to be moved up a day and another had to be played at 12:30 p.m. ET on a Thursday. But even that early game was joyful and loud, a full house of fans skipping work and school to cheer on the Dream in a must-win Game 6.

Next year, the Dream moves back to State Farm Arena full time, playing all 25 regular-season home games there.

And as disappointed as the Dream were after losing Game 7, they also immediately expressed excitement about the 2027 season.

"Just because we didn't win today doesn't mean that we won't be champions in the future," Reese said.

Those words weren't just platitudes after a disappointing ending. Next year, with every starter already signed to return, the Dream could at last win that elusive title.

"I like our chemistry and just the sisterhood that we have as a team," said Gray, who played every Finals game despite sustaining an injury on her shooting hand in the semifinals. "We actually love each other and enjoy being around each other."

stories.headline: Best of MLB playoffs: Moments, games that defined October
stories.summary: A week after the Brewers completed their title run, here's what we won't soon forget from the 2026 postseason.
stories.body:
Whether you love dramatic finishes, thrilling moments or incredible individual performances, the 2026 MLB playoffs provided a little bit of everything.

A week after the Milwaukee Brewers lifted their first World Series championship trophy, we asked our MLB experts to pick the best single moments, games and series from the entire postseason -- along with their lasting October impressions.

From wild-card thrillers to World Series heroics, here is the best of the best from every round of the 2026 postseason.

What was the defining moment of the entire MLB playoffs?

Bradford Doolittle: As it turned out, I was at all the Brewers' playoff games except the two in San Diego. So I was there when Ty France launched a ball off the American Family Field ceiling, or some wires or whatever, and Jackson Chourio stuck with the play and caught it and the Brewers won. All through the rest of the postseason, Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy alluded to the play as Bob Uecker reaching down from the great beyond to swat that ball down to help the Brewers.

I can't get on board with that, but at the same time it was a moment when I felt like Milwaukee was destined to win. And all through the Brewers' run, it felt like so many borderline moments, whether resolved by luck or skill, went Milwaukee's way. You take baseball's best team and then give it the majority of the breaks and you have what we ended up with: a champion that went 11-2 en route to winning it all.

David Schoenfield: Given the strength of the top teams in the NL compared to the obvious weaknesses of the best AL teams, it felt like the NLCS between the Brewers and Dodgers was going to decide the eventual World Series champ. After losing Game 1 with Tarik Skubal, the Dodgers at least knew they had 2025 postseason hero Yoshinobu Yamamoto going in Game 2. Then came the bottom of the third inning and Jake Bauers' walk.

How can a walk be the defining moment of the MLB playoffs? Because it was a 12-pitch walk with Bauers grinding and battling and fouling off six pitches with a 3-2 count before finally drawing ball four. It wiped out Yamamoto. Christian Yelich followed with a go-ahead two-run single and Yamamoto was out of the game, unable to finish the inning. The Dodgers would actually retake the lead, but with Yamamoto gone early, the Brewers went back ahead against the Dodgers' second-line relievers. The Brewers had won games that Skubal and Yamamoto started. Neither would throw another pitch.

Jeff Passan: If anything encapsulated the 2026 Milwaukee Brewers, it was the fifth inning of Game 3 of the World Series. After Christian Yelich's excellent baserunning instincts saved the inning from ending on a force play at second, the Brewers rapped two-out hit after two-out hit en route to scoring eight runs and extending a 2-0 advantage to 10-0. This wasn't a moment, per se; it was 26 minutes of horror for Tampa Bay. And those minutes birthed a moment that's undeniable: the one in which the Rays understood just how different the Brewers really were.

What was the single best game of the entire MLB postseason?

Buster Olney: The Padres could've upended the Brewers' championship run in the division series between the two teams, and it looked like they might be in position to do that in Game 2, when they handed a 3-2 lead to the most feared closer in the game, Mason Miller.

The right-hander, asked to get the last six outs, zipped through three Milwaukee hitters in the eighth, needing only 12 pitches. But in the ninth, the Brewers' hitters did what they became known for in October: grinding through at-bats. With Miller suddenly struggling to command his fastball, Christian Yelich worked a walk, and after Yelich stole second, Sal Frelick walked. Then Miller's slider began to flatten out as his pitch count mounted, and pinch hitter Gary Sanchez stared him down for another walk, loading the bases.

Miller's pitch count had climbed over 30, and with his slider failing him, he leaned into his fastball against Jackson Chourio - and the 22-year-old swung confidently, aggressively. Miller's 40th pitch was a 101 mph fastball, and Chourio lashed a single to center to drive in the winning run. From that point forward, no one seriously threatened the Brewers.

Alden Gonzalez: This might not have been the best game of the postseason, per se, but it's one that shouldn't be lost to history. The Braves decided to push their ace, Chris Sale, back to Game 3 of the NLDS, a risky decision that felt calamitous after the Dodgers took Game 1.

Atlanta's hopes of maintaining a reasonable chance of winning the series would fall on the shoulders of its bullpen. And then Ray Kerr, a minor league journeyman who famously once worked at 7-Eleven, and Didier Fuentes, a 20-year-old who graduated to the big leagues much earlier than expected, combined for 19 of the Braves' 27 outs in an improbable victory, delivering 6⅓ innings of one-run ball.

The Braves went on to lose the next two games and were thus eliminated, but Game 2 of the NLDS was a reminder of what makes postseason baseball so great -- the surprises that define October, the guys you've never heard of who become heroes.

Jorge Castillo: The Brewers won the World Series in five games, but the matchup was plenty closer than that indicates. Three of the five games were decided by one run, including my pick for the best game of the postseason: Game 4 at Tropicana Field.

Tampa Bay appeared on its way to getting swept when Cooper Pratt homered off Ian Seymour in the 12th inning to give the Brewers a 3-2 lead and move them within three outs of the first championship in franchise history. But the Rays, after not scoring since the fourth inning, scored two runs on an error and four straight singles without recording an out to keep their season alive.

The teams combined to use 15 pitchers. The Rays emptied their bench. Ben Williamson, the final player off that bench, delivered the walk-off single -- a ball that bounced off the artificial turf in front of home plate and into shallow right field. For one night, the Rays had hope.

What was the best series of the playoffs, from any round?

Jesse Rogers: If you can believe it, there were only two series that went the distance this October: The Braves beating the Phillies in the wild-card round and the Guardians outlasting the White Sox in their division series matchup.

The latter turned out to be one of the best of October as it featured a little bit of everything: Road teams winning the first four games, come-from-behind victories and dramatic moments -- like when Cleveland lefty Erik Sabrowski struck out Munetaka Murakami with the bases loaded in Game 5. Both fan bases were energized throughout the series, providing more energy in the building than some other contests in October. Oh, and Cleveland stormed back from 2-0 in the series to win it. It was a good one.

Olney: The Padres were the hottest team in the majors the last two months of the regular season, and in the divisional round, they faced the best team from 2026, the Brewers. It felt to a lot of folks in the game that the eventual champion would emerge from this series, and after some great moments -- Chourio's game-winning hit off Miller in Game 2, Garrett Mitchell intercepting a would-be home run in Petco Park -- Milwaukee survived the Padres and went 8-1 in its remaining postseason games.

Gonzalez: Buster is correct. There was no better series than Brewers-Padres. It lasted only four games, but every one of them contained a defining moment (don't forget Game 3, when Michael King, pitching two days after his start, took down the last two innings to save the Padres' season on a night when both Adrian Morejon and Mason Miller were unavailable).

The Brewers went on to sweep the Dodgers in the NLCS and breeze past the Rays in the final round. By the end, it was clear that the Padres were their biggest challenge. If any one moment goes the other way -- France's fly ball, Chourio's at-bat, King's appearance, Machado's fly ball -- we might be looking at a different World Series champion right now.

What is your lasting takeaway of this MLB postseason?

Passan: The return of small-market, low-payroll teams to the apex of the sport amid a labor negotiation in which the owners continue to suggest small-market, low-payroll teams can't compete in the current environment. The league's point about the recent history of World Series participants coming from larger markets and payrolls is fair, but multiple owners, speaking on the condition of anonymity, acknowledged that the Brewers and Rays facing off in the World Series did little to help reinforce their argument that a salary cap's main purpose would serve competitive balance.

Schoenfield: The perception -- incorrect -- that the Brewers were some scrappy, small-ball team that punched above its weight and slapped the ball around to victory. Nonsense. Yes, the Brewers have made some wonderful moves through the years to obtain players other teams didn't want, especially flipping Josh Hader for Robert Gasser (their Game 3 starter) and Esteury Ruiz, who was later traded for William Contreras. They got closer Trevor Megill for nothing, and Jake Bauers emerged off the scrap heap to have a star turn in 2026.

But this team has talented players up and down the roster: Brice Turang was a first-round pick in 2018, Garrett Mitchell in 2020, Sal Frelick in 2021. Yelich, Andrew Vaughn and DL Hall were first-round picks by other organizations. Cooper Pratt was a sixth-round pick, but regarded as a first-round talent and signed for second-round money. Jacob Misiorowski was a second-round pick. Jackson Chourio was the No. 2 prospect in the game. Luis Lara is a 21-year-old speedster who can run everything down in the outfield.

Yes, the Brewers have a different style -- they had the highest ground ball rate in the majors -- but they still hit the ball hard. They had the seventh-highest average exit velocity in the regular season and the third-most balls hit at 100-plus mph. They draw walks -- second-most in the regular season and 15 more than their opponents during the postseason. Most of the position players can run as well. They draft athletes and develop them and get their pitchers to throw harder or throw more strikes.

They actually struck out a few more times than their opponents during the playoffs. Sure, they hit "only" 13 home runs in 14 playoff games -- but they outhomered their opponents 13-4. They won with scouting, player development, execution, plate discipline and enough home run power. They have good baseball players. That's why they won.

Doolittle: As soon as the World Series matchup was set, I was fixated on the television ratings. I wasn't so much concerned with comparisons to the past two years, which both featured ideal conditions to produce big ratings. I was really curious how they would compare to 2023 -- the Rangers-Diamondbacks matchup that did not fare well in the ratings game. It was a short series, like this one, and also didn't feature markets favored by television, or at least as I understand the subject.

This series by all accounts fared way better than that one, with around 11.7 million viewers on average as compared to around 9.1 million in 2023. Here is my contention: People were thrilled by this matchup and this was true because of how these teams play baseball and, most crucially, because they were the respective top seeds in their leagues. It was the same matchup we would have gotten if we were still using the format in place from 1903 to 1968. In 2023, by contrast, we were watching a 5-seed against a 6-seed.

I think this matters -- a lot -- and I think favoring a format that rewards regular season excellence should be paramount when we consider such things going forward.

stories.headline: Robert Lewandowski's jersey outselling Lionel Messi's since Chicago arrival
stories.summary: Robert Lewandowski's Chicago Fire jersey has been the most popular in MLS since his arrival to the league in June, outselling even Lionel Messi's Miami kit.
stories.body:
Robert Lewandowski's Chicago Fire jersey has been the most popular in Major League Soccer since his arrival to the league in June, outselling even Lionel Messi's Inter Miami kit.

MLS' 10 best-selling jerseys of 2026 was revealed by the league on Tuesday, with Messi still No. 1 overall but with former Barcelona and Bayern Munich star Lewandowski making a big impact.

- MLS Power Rankings: Miami finds its feet with Decision Day coming up

- Messi brings Miami back to stun Revs, clinch Champions Cup spot

- Nashville ties Miami's single-season points record with 1 game to go

Lewandowski officially signed with Chicago on June 29, and made his MLS debut on July 22 against Inter Miami.

The Poland international has recorded seven goals and added five assists in 18 games, propelling the Fire to fourth place on the Eastern Conference table and a place in the playoffs.

Miami captain Messi, however, leads sales through all of 2026, earning first place for the fourth consecutive season. Messi first topped the list in 2023, just months after signing with Inter Miami in July of that year.

This year, just behind Messi, LAFC's Son Heung-Min stands in second place and Vancouver Whitecaps forward Thomas Müller in third.

The list was based on sales made on MLS' online store from Jan. 1 through Oct. 30.

New Orlando City player Antoine Griezmann made the list in fifth place after being announced as a new signing in March but officially joining MLS in July upon completing the 2025-26 season with Atlético Madrid.

In sixth place was rising United States star Cavan Sullivan's Philadelphia Union jersey. Sullivan, 17, became the youngest scorer for the U.S. men's national team last month when he found the net against Mexico.

stories.headline: Luana Santos comes to grips with rise in women's bantamweight rankings
stories.summary: Here's a look at every weight class to determine the best of the best in UFC, PFL and beyond.
stories.body:
Luana Santos stuck with her strongest fighting skill -- grappling -- in Saturday's UFC fight with fellow top-10 women's bantamweight Yana Santos. Her perseverance paid off. After all nine of her takedown attempts were fended off in the first round, Santos went right back to leaning on her judo background in the two rounds that followed, landing five takedowns and amassing 7½ minutes of control time and winning her fourth fight in a row.

As a result, Luana Santos climbs two spots to No. 5 in the ESPN women's bantamweight rankings, while previously fifth-ranked Yana Santos drops one position to No. 6.

That is the only change in the latest divisional rankings. Women's bantamweight does have change on the horizon, though, as UFC champion Kayla Harrison, unranked because she has not fought in over a year and is ineligible, takes on former two-division champion Amanda Nunes on Nov. 14 at UFC 334. Nunes is coming off a retirement of nearly 3½ years.

Here are the ESPN pound-for-pound MMA rankings and a list of current UFC champions in all weight classes.

Results are current; rankings as of Nov. 3. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

stories.headline: Kiwis gun reveals key to Ponga miracle
stories.summary: Superstar fullback Kayln Ponga has the captain's run to prove his fitness and make a miraculous return from a broken arm to play in NZ's World Cup semi-final.
stories.body:
Jahrome Hughes had a blinder for Melbourne 22 days after breaking his arm last year and says Kalyn Ponga is on track to make his own stunning comeback for New Zealand, if he can tick one key box.

Ponga, named on an extended bench for the Kiwis in Saturday night's semi-final at Newcastle's McDonald Jones Stadium, trained strongly on Wednesday.

Coach Stacey Jones said Ponga had "a few boxes to tick" as he leant on the advice of Hughes.

Ponga played for more than 20 minutes with his injury in New Zealand's epic tournament-opening 24-22 loss to Australia, before undergoing surgery in the hope of returning for the finals.

Kiwis halfback Hughes broke his arm against Brisbane in a final-round game in 2025, before returning for the preliminary final to inspire a victory over Cronulla.

He said there was "one thing I told KP" that would be vital for Ponga to get back for the clash with red-hot Tonga, just 23 days after his own fracture..

"(Storm) had a week off after we won that first final, and we had a full opposed session and I wanted to get a full contact session in," Hughes said.

"That gave me all the confidence in the world that a week later I'd be able to do my job on the field. If I wasn't able to do that I wouldn't have played.

"(Ponga) has got to have confidence in his arm and feel right. You don't want him to worry about his arm the whole game because that will take away from his game.

"He is training really well. That's another step towards playing."

Jones kept his cards close to his chest when asked if Ponga would start the match if fit.

"We will get through one more session and see where it goes. Kalyn is looking pretty good," he said.

Ponga and fellow Newcastle fan favourite Phoenix Crossland, also named on an extended bench, could spell double trouble for Tonga.

A month after playing together in Newcastle's 19-18 NRL grand final loss to the Sydney Roosters, centre Dane Gagai is backing the former Dally M Medallist to terrorise Tonga, in what would be a huge boost for the Kiwis.

"That'll just come down to the boxes he'll have to tick with the physios and stuff, but one thing that's never in question is Kalyn's toughness and I don't think he gets enough credit or praise for it," Gagai said.

"Some of the games he's played with injury. It was only maybe a year or two ago with his AC (acromioclavicular joint) and getting that injected, but he'll put his head in most places that people won't put their hands.

"So I've got no doubt he'll do everything he can to make sure he can take that field. It's just a case of whether he can tick those boxes and he'll know whether he's capable of playing or not.

"He won't put himself before the team, but we'd obviously love to have him out there."

Jones said Crossland could also be a late inclusion, after completing a four-game suspension for a hip-drop tackle that broke Nathan Cleary's ankle in Newcastle's preliminary final victory over Penrith.

Knowing New Zealand will need their strongest possible line-up to keep Tonga at bay, Gagai also welcomed the prospect of the classy hooker featuring in the do-or-die showdown.

"He's come in a bit later into camp, but even though he wasn't playing he's always himself and brings a lot of energy," Gagai said.

"He's awesome to have around the place. It's going to be good to be able to chuck this jersey on with him and nice to know that the game against Penrith wasn't our last together.

"So I'm definitely looking forward to that and I'm super happy for him."

stories.headline: NFL Week 9 betting odds: Lines and totals for every game
stories.summary: Odds, spreads, totals and FPI predictions for every NFL game in Week 9.
stories.body:
Week 9 gets underway with the Baltimore Ravens hosting the Jacksonville Jaguars on Thursday night at M&T Bank Stadium. The Ravens, who will be without Lamar Jackson, are early 10-point home underdogs.
